title: Social Movements
tagline: Reform movements of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries and the social questions they put on the national agenda.

overview.intro: Colonial rule disturbed Indian society in ways it had not expected: traditional authorities weakened, new education and print created new publics, and reformers argued for change both from within Indian tradition and from contact with European ideas. This unit examines the social movements that reshaped nineteenth-century India, from the Brahmo Samaj and the Arya Samaj to the work of Vivekananda and the movement for widow remarriage and women’s education, together with the conservative responses that met them. The examination value lies in connecting each movement to the specific reform it pursued.

learn.title: The Brahmo Samaj and the movement for reform

blocks.text: Raja Ram Mohan Roy founded the Brahmo Samaj in 1828 as a monotheistic movement that drew on the Upanishads while rejecting image worship and priestly ritual. Its most celebrated success was the campaign against sati, which Roy argued was no sanctioned Hindu practice and which the colonial government abolished by regulation in 1829. The movement pressed for a wider programme too: education in English and in the vernacular, the abolition of caste privilege, the remarriage of widows, and the end of polygamy. After Roy’s death, Keshab Chandra Sen led the Samaj in a more radical direction, which split it in 1866 into the more conservative Adi Brahmo Samaj and the Calcutta faction.

learn.title: The Arya Samaj and the Ramakrishna Mission

blocks.text: Swami Dayananda Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj in 1875, insisting on the authority of the Vedas as infallible and rejecting image worship, caste by birth and the authority of later scripture. Its slogan, back to the Vedas, was a call to recover what it saw as an original social equality, and the movement ran schools, opened the door of the upper castes to the so-called untouchable communities, and supported widow remarriage. The movement’s shuddhi ceremony aimed at reconversion and it later influenced the nationalist assertion of a self-confident Hindu identity.

Swami Vivekananda gave the Ramakrishna Mission its institutional form in 1897, four years after his address at the Parliament of Religions in Chicago in 1893 had presented Hinduism to a world audience. The Mission combined spiritual training with practical service: schools, dispensaries, disaster relief and famine work, on the principle that service to man was service to God. Vivekananda’s contribution to nationalism was cultural rather than political, arguing that the strength of the nation lay in its people and that social service, not mere ritual, was true religion.

learn.title: Women’s education, the Phules and the conservative response

blocks.text: Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar campaigned for widow remarriage with such effect that the Widow Remarriage Act was passed in 1856, and he also opened schools for girls. In western India, Jyotirao Phule and his wife Savitribai Phule founded schools for girls and for lower castes in the 1840s, and Phule’s Gulamgiri attacked the caste order directly by arguing that the so-called upper castes were themselves outsiders. The women’s movement acquired an organised form later, with the formation of the Women’s Indian Association in 1917 and the presentation of petitions for female suffrage.

Reform met organised resistance. Opponents argued that change was being imposed from outside and that scriptural sanction existed for the practices attacked. Conservative leaders warned that reform would weaken social discipline, and some communities formed associations to resist conversion and what they saw as westernisation. Colonial policy itself was ambivalent, since officials hesitated to interfere with what they called native custom, and reforms were carried through only when Indian reformers built sufficient pressure. The debate established a pattern that continued into the freedom struggle: every social question was argued in the language of both tradition and modernity.

learn.title: Assessment: achievements and limits of the reform movements

blocks.text: The achievements were concrete. Sati was abolished in 1829 and widow remarriage legalised in 1856, both after sustained Indian argument rather than by unilateral colonial initiative. Girls’ schools became an accepted feature of the urban landscape, caste was publicly attacked as a principle for the first time in much of northern India, and the movements created a permanent public sphere in which social questions were debated in newspapers, lectures and associations. Reform also gave Indians practice in the politics of petition, organisation and publicity that the national movement later used.

The limits were equally real. Most of the movements were led by and addressed to the educated upper and middle castes of the cities, so their reach into the countryside and among the lower castes was narrow. Where the colonial state acted, it usually acted on a narrow point of law rather than on the structure of land, labour or caste that produced the inequality. Several movements also turned inward: the later Arya Samaj emphasis on shuddhi and the conservative response to reform show how easily a reforming impulse could become a question of community identity rather than social change. An exam answer that lists reforms without weighing their reach loses the assessment marks that distinguish a strong response.

questions.prompt: The Brahmo Samaj was founded in 1828 by:
questions.explanation: Ram Mohan Roy founded the Brahmo Samaj as a monotheistic movement that rejected image worship and priestly ritual.

questions.prompt: The Widow Remarriage Act was passed in:
questions.explanation: The Act of 1856 followed Vidyasagar’s long campaign and the petitioning of the Bengal government.

questions.prompt: The slogan back to the Vedas is associated with:
questions.explanation: Dayananda Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj in 1875 on the authority of the Vedas alone.

questions.prompt: Which pair correctly matches a reformer with the reform he is most closely associated with?
options: Vidyasagar and the abolition of sati
Ram Mohan Roy and the abolition of sati
questions.answer: Ram Mohan Roy and the abolition of sati
questions.explanation: Ram Mohan Roy campaigned most forcefully against sati before the regulation of 1829, while Vidyasagar is tied to widow remarriage.

questions.prompt: The movement founded by Swami Vivekananda in 1897 that combined spiritual training with social service is the Ramakrishna __________ .
questions.explanation: The Mission ran schools, dispensaries and relief work on the principle that service to people was service to God.

questions.prompt: The ceremony of __________ promoted by the Arya Samaj aimed at reconversion to Hinduism.
questions.explanation: Shuddhi was the reverse of conversion and became an important part of the movement’s social programme.

questions.prompt: State four reforms demanded by the Brahmo Samaj.
questions.answer: Four demands are: the abolition of sati as neither scripturally required nor voluntary; the remarriage of widows, who were otherwise condemned to lifelong suffering; education for women, since ignorance kept them dependent; and opposition to caste hierarchy, because birth-based superiority contradicted a single creator. Education in English and the vernacular is also accepted.
questions.explanation: Each demand needs the reason the reformers gave, since the reasoning is what distinguishes a strong answer.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between the Arya Samaj and the Ramakrishna Mission.
questions.answer: The Arya Samaj, founded in 1875, held the Vedas to be infallible and sought reform through argument, education and the shuddhi ceremony, opposing caste by birth and image worship. The Ramakrishna Mission, founded in 1897 by Vivekananda, rested on personal experience and the teachings of Ramakrishna and worked through service such as schools, dispensaries and relief. The Arya Samaj was argumentative and textual while the Mission was practical and service oriented, though both sought a renewal of Hindu society.
questions.explanation: Three points of contrast are required, each drawn as a difference rather than a description of one movement.

questions.prompt: Explain the contribution of Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar and Jyotirao Phule to social reform.
questions.answer: Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar campaigned for the remarriage of widows, arguing from scripture that the practice had been permitted in earlier ages and combining that precedent with a humanitarian case. His petitioning and public writing were decisive in the passage of the Widow Remarriage Act of 1856, and he also established schools for girls at a time when female education attracted hostility. Jyotirao Phule, working in western India with his wife Savitribai, opened schools for girls and for lower castes in the 1840s, which was a far more radical act since it challenged caste as well as gender. In Gulamgiri he argued that the oppressed castes were the original inhabitants and that the hierarchy imposed on them was a conquest, so his reform linked education with a structural critique of caste. Both reformers therefore attacked the position of women and the lower orders together, and both met resistance, with Phule’s schools facing boycott and Vidyasagar’s campaign attracting organised opposition.
questions.explanation: Full marks need both reformers with their specific achievements and the social context that made each action difficult.

questions.prompt: Reform in nineteenth-century India was as much resistance as change. Explain this statement with reference to opposition to the abolition of sati and to girls’ education.
questions.answer: The statement holds because every reform challenged an interest and a worldview, so it provoked an organised defence. Sati was resisted on the grounds that the colonial state had no business interfering with native custom, that the practice was scripturally sanctioned, and that abolition would undermine the authority of the priesthood and the honour code of the families concerned. The reformers answered by showing that the ritual was rarely voluntary, that it was often encouraged by those who benefited from it, and that scripture did not require it, and the regulation of 1829 therefore represented not an external imposition but an internal argument that had won the support of the state. Girls’ education met a different resistance: schools were attacked, families feared that educated girls would be unmarriageable, and conservative opinion held that female learning would destabilise the household. Reformers met this by opening schools quietly, securing royal and later official patronage, and demonstrating that educated women produced stable households rather than disorder. In both cases reform required resistance because the practice being changed was protected by custom, interest and authority together, and the eventual change came only when reformers built enough public argument to move the state.
questions.explanation: Marks are for showing that resistance was structured and specific, and that the reformers answered each objection on its own terms.
